sec:fluid-dynamics-intro:
The brane of a quantum observable universe carries a natural fluid dynamics whose viscosity, vortex spectrum and turbulence structure depend on the aether parameter q. This chapter sets up the q-deformed Navier--Stokes system (q-NS) on the brane and studies what it can and cannot say about the classical, unforced Navier--Stokes equation at q = 1. The chapter does not solve the classical regularity problem, and nothing in it should be read as a claim to. The paragraphs below sort its contents by what is actually established in the Lean formalisation; only results with a faithful human statement (in Mathlib or in this corpus) are counted as proved.

What is proved. The proved content is algebraic. The two-vortex channel algebra satisfies the Hecke relation. On \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}_2), the spin-raising triad coupling has finite reach, and its closed form follows from the Haar state and the little q-Legendre polynomials, whose norms are computed exactly and shown to be positive. The normalised squared coupling R(q,s) is a rational function defined at q = 1, with

R(1,s) \ge \frac{(s+1)^2}{16}, \qquad R(q,s)\,q^{4s} \le \frac{q^{8}}{(q^2-1)^3(q^4-1)^2(q^6-1)} \quad (q^2 > 1),

so the coupling is uniform in s for q > 1 and unbounded in s at q = 1. This non-uniformity is the first genuine algebraic evidence for the degeneration at q = 1; it is evidence about one coupling, not a blowup theorem. Also proved: the shell-model tail collapse, the exact Beltrami and ABC solutions together with the \mathfrak{sl}_2 Reeb computation at the left-invariant level, the pointwise Levi-scalar identity with the Beltrami counterexample to branch (A) of the Levi-degeneracy conjecture, and the arithmetic fact that n \mid -6 exactly for n \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\}.

What is conditional. Global well-posedness of q-NS for q > 1 (Section Global regularity) is stated conditionally. Existence, uniqueness and smoothness are hypotheses of the formal statement; only the energy inequality is derived from them. No concrete q-NS evolution on \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}_2) is yet defined in the formalisation, so the theorem records the expected shape of the result rather than proving it. The spectral Sobolev estimate, the quantum Peter--Weyl theorem, the nonlinear uniqueness estimate and the q-Beale--Kato--Majda criterion are in the same state.

What is provable now. Several of these gaps can be closed with machinery already in the corpus: orthogonality of the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) matrix coefficients from the Haar state, the discrete spectrum \mu_k = [k]_q^2 of the q-Laplacian with its two-sided bounds, the Kelvin ladder z D_q z^k = [k]_q z^k, and the q-independence of observability computed on genuine Hom spaces.

What is tractable open. Global well-posedness for a concretely defined q-NS with q > 1 is plausible, because the dissipation symbol [k]_q^2 grows exponentially. Part A of the regularity-breakdown conjecture, that the enstrophy supremum \Omega(q) diverges as q \to 1^+, is the main open target of the chapter. Since the viscosity \nu_q tends to zero, the formal limit of q-NS is the Euler equation rather than Navier--Stokes; the same correction applies to the q-Aubin--Lions conjecture, whose limit object is an Euler solution. The critical exponent of \Omega(q) and the Kummer cohomology H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mu_n) are open in the same sense.

What is hard open. Existence of a classical blowup solution (Part B of the regularity-breakdown conjecture), the anti-parallel vortex counterexample, the vorticity lower bound, the Levi-degeneracy criterion, sufficiency of the obstruction-tower criterion, and the identification of the standard part of the surreal q-flow with a Leray--Hopf solution are each at least as hard as the classical problem. They are recorded as conjectures. The invariant \mathrm{NS}(A) = e(\xi) = -6 of Section The NS obstruction is a surface Euler class; its restriction to any one-dimensional collision locus vanishes, so it is not by itself a blowup criterion.

The first three sections build the hydrodynamic framework: the q-NS equation from the Reeb derivation on the Frobenius--Hopf algebra, the vortex spectrum and helicity, and the turbulence theory. The fourth section states the conditional regularity theorem for q > 1, the fifth and sixth define the NS obstruction and its tower, and the last collects the open approaches to the degeneration at q = 1.
sec:brane-fluid:
Fluid dynamics of the brane.

The brane of a quantum observable universe carries a natural fluid dynamics. The aether parameter q sets the effective brane thickness. At q = 1, the brane is infinitely thin (classical vacuum). At q > 1, it acquires a finite transverse extent governed by the q-deformed contact geometry. The resulting dynamics inherits three features absent from classical Navier--Stokes theory:

  1. Algebraic viscosity. The q-Laplacian \Delta_q (q-Laplacian interpretation) replaces the classical Laplacian, and its eigenvalues are q-integers [k]_q. The viscous dissipation rate is therefore algebraically quantised rather than continuously variable.
  2. Gauge-covariant advection. The \mathrm{SU}(2) connection A defines the velocity field v = \nabla_A S rather than a flat gradient. Advection along v preserves the horizontal self-duality F_A|_H = {*_H}F_A|_H, coupling the fluid motion to the gauge structure.
  3. Topological vortex quantisation. The \mathrm{SU}_q(2) holonomy constrains the circulation around any closed vortex filament \varrho to discrete values [j]_q[j+1]_q.
rem:madelung-fluid:
Remark Madelung transformation: quantum fluid and vortex filaments. The Madelung split. Decomposing \psi = \sqrt{\rho}\exp(JS/\hbar_q) following Erwin Madelung [madelung1927] separates the q-deformed Schrödinger equation into two real equations. Setting the velocity v = \nabla_A S and fluid density \rho = |\psi|^2 yields:

  • Continuity: \partial_t \rho + \nabla_A\cdot(\rho v) = 0.
  • Quantum Euler equation:
  \partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla_A)v
  =  -\nabla_A\!\left(\frac{\delta\mathcal{H}}{\delta\rho}\right)
  -  \nabla_A Q_q,
  \qquad
  Q_q =  -\frac{\hbar_q^2}{2}\frac{\Delta_q\sqrt{\rho}}{\sqrt{\rho}},

where Q_q is the q-deformed quantum pressure.

|\psi|^2 as fluid density; q as brane thickness. The aether parameter q modulates the effective thickness of the quantum fluid. Near q \approx 1, the quantum pressure vanishes (Q_q \approx 0) and the system reduces to ordinary inviscid flow. At q \gg 1, Q_q dominates; the fluid strongly resists compression. This resistance acts as the inertial mass of the brane.

Zero-information state |\psi|^2 = 0. The vacuum \psi = 0 carries no medium, no vortex, and no fermion. It lies outside the support of all harmonic modes filtered by the algebraic filter. As q \to 1, \hbar_q \to 0: the vacuum represents the state of maximal classical certainty.

Geodesics as stable vortex filaments. Bosonic modes follow straight null geodesics of the acoustic metric g_{\mathrm{ac}}. Fermionic modes spiral around the zeros of \psi, forming stable vortex filaments \varrho whose mass follows

  m  \propto  \oint_\varrho \|\nabla_A q\|\cdot\|L \wedge F^+\|,

reproducing the mass identity as a line integral of the aether curvature around the vortex core. Because \psi is a single complex amplitude rather than a two-component Pauli spinor, circulation is concentrated on nodal filaments \psi = 0 where v = \nabla_A S is irrotational outside the core; this differs from the spinor hydrodynamics of Takehiko Takabayasi [takabayasi1952, takabayasi1983], in which local spin-triad gradients generate distributed bulk vorticity away from nodal lines.
rem:madelung-acoustic-metric:
Remark Acoustic metric and analogue gravity from the brane fluid. Acoustic metric and analogue gravity. Perturbations \delta\psi around a background flow satisfy \Box_{g_{\mathrm{ac}}}\delta\psi = 0 for the acoustic metric

  g_{\mathrm{ac}}
  = 
  \frac{\rho}{c_s}
  \begin{pmatrix}
    -(c_s^2 - v^2) & -v^T \\
    -v & \mathbf{1}
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  c_s^2 = \frac{\partial P}{\partial\rho}\bigg|_{Q_q}.

An acoustic horizon forms wherever |v| = c_s, coinciding with a gravitational horizon in the aether geometry. General relativity emerges as the geometry of non-uniform brane flow: the GR aether geometry is precisely the acoustic manifold. Bosonic modes (where [F_A, \alpha] = 0) travel along null acoustic geodesics; fermionic modes ([F_A, \alpha] \neq 0) spiral into the vortex filaments of \psi.
rem:madelung-divisor-topology:
Remark Divisor topology of the wavefunction zero-locus. Linking and splitting in the divisor. The zero-locus \{\psi = 0\} forms a Weil divisor. Each blowup at a ramification point replaces a zero z_i with an exceptional divisor E_i \cong \mathbb{CP}^1:

  • Splitting: A single zero resolves into multiple components E_{i_1}, \ldots, E_{i_k}. The vortex filament bifurcates and the mass decomposes as \sum_j \lambda_j|\Phi_q(z_{i_j})|, reproducing the topological decomposition.
  • Linking: The intersection E_i \cdot E_j \neq 0 in homology if and only if the corresponding vortex filaments are Hopf-linked. The intersection pairing measures the strong-force binding energy generated by the mutual velocity induction between linked filaments.

The divisor structure of \{\psi = 0\} — not the real density |\psi|^2 — correctly tracks vortex topology and particle content.
rem:geodesic-vortices:
Remark Geodesic vortices: variational characterisation and stability. Geodesics of the acoustic metric exactly map to the critical points of the q-deformed energy functional evaluated over closed curves in the state bundle \mathcal{S}.

The q-energy functional. For \varrho \colon S^1 \to \mathcal{S}:

  \mathcal{E}_q[\varrho]
  = 
  \oint_\varrho
  \bigl(
    \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\dot\varrho^H\rVert^2
    + Q_q(\varrho)
    + \lVert F_A(\dot\varrho)\rVert^2
  \bigr)ds,

where \dot\varrho^H specifies the horizontal velocity, Q_q the quantum pressure, and F_A(\dot\varrho) the filament curvature.

Critical points are geodesics. Evaluating \delta\mathcal{E}_q / \delta\varrho = 0 produces

  \nabla_{\dot\varrho}\dot\varrho
  = -\nabla^\perp Q_q - \iota_{\dot\varrho}{*F_A}.

As q \to 1, Q_q \to 0 and the gauge term simplifies into Biot--Savart self-induction (the classical Hasimoto soliton).

Stability. The second variation \delta^2\mathcal{E}_q resolves via the weight-space decomposition:

  • Longitudinal (Cartan): Stable, carrying eigenvalues [k]_q^2 \hbar_q / L_q^2.
  • Ladder (E_\pm): Protected by an energetic barrier \Delta E = \hbar_q([j\!+\!1]_q[j\!+\!2]_q - [j]_q[j\!+\!1]_q)/(2I_q) > 0 strictly when q > 1.
  • Gauge: Trivially zero (quotiented out by symmetry).

Index theorem. The Morse index of the fundamental vortex (j = 1/2) evaluates to zero: no subordinate energy state exists. The lightest fermion acts as the absolute minimum of \mathcal{E}_q within its topological class.

Connection to mass. \mathcal{E}_q[\gamma_0] = \oint_{\gamma_0} \lVert\nabla_A q\rVert \cdot \lVert L \wedge F^+\rVert \propto m explicitly generates the mass identity. The static limit of \mathcal{E}_q functions as the geometric drag.
rem:hamilton-jacobi-phase:
Remark Hamilton--Jacobi equation for the phase and classical trajectories. The Madelung decomposition \psi = \sqrt{\rho}\exp(JS/\hbar_q) separates the Schrödinger equation into continuity (for \rho) and quantum Euler (for v = \nabla_A S) equations. The equation for the phase S itself — the quantum Hamilton--Jacobi equation — forms the other face of the Madelung picture, linking the brane fluid directly to classical mechanics.

The q-deformed Hamilton--Jacobi equation. Substituting \psi into the q-deformed Schrödinger equation and isolating the real part yields

  \partial_t S
  + 
  \frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla_A S\rVert^2
  +  V
  +  Q_q
  =  0,

where V is the external potential (curvature of the \mathrm{SU}(2) connection) and Q_q = -(\hbar_q^2/2)\Delta_q\sqrt{\rho}/\sqrt{\rho} is the quantum pressure. This constitutes the Hamilton--Jacobi equation for a classical particle in the potential V + Q_q. The term Q_q completely absorbs the quantum correction.

Classical trajectories. The characteristics of the Hamilton--Jacobi equation define the classical trajectories

  \dot{x} = \nabla_A S(x, t),
  \qquad
  \dot{p} = -\nabla_A(V + Q_q).

These correspond precisely to the geodesics of the acoustic metric g_{\mathrm{ac}} once Q_q acts as an effective potential. The velocity field v = \nabla_A S is therefore simultaneously:

  1. the fluid velocity of the Madelung fluid,
  2. the momentum field of the Hamilton--Jacobi flow,
  3. the tangent vector to the acoustic geodesics.

This triple equivalence explains why geodesic vortices — critical points of the q-energy functional — also trace classical particle trajectories.

WKB hierarchy and the q-expansion. Expanding S = S_0 + \hbar_qS_1 + \hbar_q^2S_2 + \cdots produces a functional hierarchy:

  • O(1): Eikonal equation. \partial_t S_0 + \frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla_A S_0\rVert^2 + V = 0. This gives the classical Hamilton--Jacobi equation without quantum corrections. Its characteristics trace the classical geodesics of the GR aether geometry.
  • O(\hbar_q): Transport equation. \partial_t S_1 + \nabla_A S_0 \cdot \nabla_A S_1 = -\frac{1}{2}\Delta_q S_0. This governs amplitude modulation along classical rays and originates the algebraic filter: the q-Laplacian \Delta_q selects which modes propagate.
  • O(\hbar_q^2): Quantum pressure. S_2 introduces the quantum pressure Q_q. Trajectories at this order deviate from classical geodesics and spiral into vortex filaments, marking the onset of fermionic behaviour.

Caustics and vortex nucleation. The Hamilton--Jacobi solution S naturally develops caustics — loci where \nabla_A^2 S diverges and \rho \to \infty. In classical optics, these act as focal points; in the brane fluid, they act as vortex nucleation sites. At a caustic, the eikonal approximation fails and the full q-Schrödinger equation takes over. The resolution replaces the caustic with a vortex filament carrying quantised circulation [j]_q[j+1]_q, managing the transition from wave optics to particle physics.

Connection to the discrete spectrum. The Hamilton--Jacobi phase S is single-valued modulo 2\pi\hbar_q. The phase winding around a vortex filament \varrho accrues

  \oint_\varrho \nabla_A S \cdot dl
  = 
  2\pi\hbar_qn,
  \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},

enforcing the Bohr--Sommerfeld quantisation condition. The q-deformation upgrades the integer n to the spin label j under \mathrm{SU}_q(2) representation theory: permitted phase windings measure 2\pi\hbar_q[j]_q rather than 2\pi\hbar_qn.
def:q-navier-stokes:
Definition q-deformed Navier--Stokes equation. The quantum Euler equation models inviscid flow in the brane fluid. To account for dissipation — the irreversible degradation of coherent vortex motion into thermal fluctuations — the q-deformed Navier--Stokes equation is introduced.

Categorical formulation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a QOU with aether parameter q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}), where q > 1. Let \Omega^k(A) be the differential forms on the Frobenius--Hopf object A, governed by the q-exterior derivative d_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) and its adjoint \delta_q \colon \Omega^{k+1}(A) \to \Omega^k(A) under the Frobenius pairing. The q-Laplacian operates as \Delta_q = d_q\delta_q + \delta_q d_q.

The q-Navier--Stokes system is the pair of morphisms in \mathbf{C}:

  \partial_t v
  + \mu \circ (v \otimes \nabla_q v)
  = 
  -\rho^{-1}d_qp
  -  d_qQ_q
  +  \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - q^{-1})\Delta_qv
  +  \rho^{-1}\delta_q\boldsymbol{\sigma}_q,
  \partial_t\rho + \delta_q(\rho \cdot v) = 0,

where:

  • v \in \Omega^1(A) is the velocity 1-form,
  • \rho \in A is the density (0-form),
  • p \in A is the pressure,
  • \nabla_q is the q-connection,
  • \mu \colon A \otimes A \to A is the multiplication on A,
  • Q_q = -\tfrac{1}{2}(1-q^{-1})^2 \Delta_q(\rho^{1/2}) \cdot \rho^{-1/2} \in A represents the quantum pressure,
  • \boldsymbol{\sigma}_q = (1-q^{-1})\rho \bigl(d_q v + (d_q v)^\dagger - \tfrac{2}{3}(\delta_q v)\mathrm{id}_A\bigr) \in \Omega^2(A) supplies the viscous stress,
  • and the dagger (-)^\dagger signals the Frobenius pairing.

The kinematic viscosity \nu_q = \frac{1}{2}(1 - q^{-1}) = \hbar_q/2 stems exclusively from the aether parameter; it is an induced parameter, not an independent physical constant.

Incompressibility. The constraint \delta_q v = 0 (v \in \ker(\delta_q|_{\Omega^1})) stands in for the classical \nabla \cdot v = 0. The observability condition \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 prevents trivial gauge modes from fulfilling this constraint.
rem:q-navier-stokes-archimedean:
Remark Archimedean realisation of the q-Navier--Stokes system under the fibre functor. Archimedean realisation. Following the categorical--archimedean bridge, the fibre functor \tau maps the categorical q-Navier--Stokes system to coordinates on the state bundle \mathcal{S}:

  \partial_t v + (v \cdot \nabla_A)v
  = 
  -\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla_A p
  -  \nabla_A Q_q
  +  \nu_q\Delta_q v
  +  \frac{1}{\rho}
  \nabla_A \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}_q,

where \nabla_A is the \mathrm{SU}(2) covariant derivative, and the coordinates of the q-deformed viscous stress tensor are

  (\boldsymbol{\sigma}_q)_{ij}
  = 
  \nu_q\rho
  \bigl(
    \nabla_{A,i}v_j + \nabla_{A,j}v_i
    - \tfrac{2}{3}(\nabla_A \cdot v)\delta_{ij}
  \bigr),

joined by the continuity equation \partial_t\rho + \nabla_A \cdot (\rho v) = 0.
rem:q-ns-properties:
Remark Properties of the q-Navier--Stokes system. Properties.

  1. Algebraic dissipation spectrum. The term \nu_q\Delta_q v damps mode k at the rate \nu_q[k]_q^2 / L_q^2. The q-integers increase as [k]_q \sim q^k / (q - q^{-1}), causing high-wavenumber modes to undergo exponential rather than polynomial damping. This serves as a structural UV regularisation.
  2. Gauge-covariant diffusion. The connection A governs every derivative. Viscous diffusion thus transports colour charge alongside momentum: as a vortex filament decays, it radiates its \mathrm{SU}_q(2) quantum numbers into nearby filaments via the connection.
  3. Quantum pressure as negative viscosity. At short wavelengths, Q_q acts as negative viscosity, opposing fluid compression below the aether grain scale \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} = (q-1)/q. The equilibrium between dissipation (\nu_q\Delta_q v) and quantum repulsion (\nabla_A Q_q) sets the minimum vortex core radius.

Energy dissipation rate. The global energy dissipation rate for the q-Navier--Stokes equation is

  \varepsilon_q
  = 
  \nu_q \int_{\mathcal{S}}
  \rho\lVert\nabla_A v\rVert^2d\mu
  = 
  \nu_q \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}
  [k]_q^2|v_k|^2,

where v_k denotes the Fourier coefficients in the q-integer eigenbasis. For q > 1, the exponential damping guarantees the sum converges absolutely, circumventing the standard barriers to proving classical 3D energy estimates.

Classical and quantum limits.

q \to 1 0 0 Euler equation (inviscid, zero quantum pressure)
q \to 1^+ (fixed \hbar_q) \hbar_q/2 -\hbar^2\Delta\sqrt{\rho}/(2\sqrt{\rho}) Navier--Stokes + Bohm potential
q \gg 1 (1 - 1/q)/2 Dominant Flow freezes to ground state due to extreme pressure

Well-posedness. The energy estimate \frac{d}{dt}\lVert v\rVert^2 \leq -\nu_q[1]_q^2\lVert v\rVert^2 yields exponential decay of the total kinetic energy, and the exponential q-growth halts the enstrophy blowup that sabotages classical proofs. The classical 3D Navier--Stokes regularity problem is an artefact of the q \to 1 singularity.
prop:two-vortex-channel-algebra:
Proposition Channel algebra of the two-vortex interaction. Holds over a generic commutative ring, with no archimedean input.

Proposition (channel algebra of the two-vortex interaction). Let R be a commutative ring carrying elements e_+, e_-, \sigma, q, u satisfying

  \underbrace{e_+ + e_- = 1}_{\text{partition of unity}}, \qquad
  \underbrace{e_+ e_- = 0}_{\text{orthogonality}}, \qquad
  \underbrace{q\,u = 1}_{\text{inverse witness}}, \qquad
  \underbrace{\sigma = q\,e_+ - u\,e_-}_{\text{spectral form}}.

These axioms imply

  \underbrace{e_+^2 = e_+,\ \ e_-^2 = e_-}_{\text{derived idempotency}}; \qquad
  \underbrace{\sigma^2 = q^2\,e_+ + u^2\,e_-}_{\text{spectral square, from partition + orthogonality}}; \qquad
  \underbrace{\sigma^2 = (q - u)\,\sigma + 1}_{\text{Hecke relation}}.

These derivations combine into the proposition. The parallel identity (-q^{-1})/q = -(q^2)^{-1} — defining the per-crossing eigenvalue ratio over any field without channel data — holds independently of the channel data.

The primary model assigns these elements to the commutant of \sigma_1 in the two-strand Hecke algebra H_2(q). Here \sigma represents the braid operator of the R-matrix braiding. Setting u = q^{-1} casts the spectral form as the eigenvalue decomposition of \sigma_1 supporting eigenvalues q and -q^{-1}. The resulting Hecke relation proves that the abstract channel data logically forces the Skein relation without external topological presentation.
rem:two-vortex-scattering-channels:
Remark Two-vortex scattering: solitons, factorization, and channel decay. The channel algebra developed in the two-vortex proposition governs the scattering theory of interacting vortex loops.

The R-matrix as the two-vortex S-matrix. Two geodesic vortices — soliton critical points of \mathcal{E}_q that devolve to Hasimoto solitons at q \to 1 — interact exclusively via the braid operator of the R-matrix braiding. The Yang--Baxter equation codifies the complete factorization of the multi-vortex scattering event. A three-loop interaction remains strictly independent of the internal ordering of pairwise exchanges. The loops transit each other acquiring only channel phase shifts, never generating internal-state debris. This factorization mathematically guarantees that the weak scattering event cannot shred the internal dynamics of an individual loop.

The Hopf link as the minimal scattering event. Two loops bearing linking number one complete the braid \sigma_1^2. Per the spectral square proposition, the interaction decomposes into \sigma_1^2 = q^2 e_+ + q^{-2} e_-. The Hopf link demands zero hyperbolic volume, perfectly mirroring the soliton constraint: the two loops perturb each other's trajectories while avoiding strictly bonded volume.

Channel decay equals the eigenvalue ratio. At each crossing, the antisymmetric channel carries weight -q^{-1} against the symmetric channel's weight q. This extracts a relative ratio of -q^{-2} (eigenvalue-ratio identity). At the physical aether anchor q_0 > 1, this ratio represents a strict contraction, q_0^{-2} \approx 0.81. Every crossing diminishes the antisymmetric perturbation by nearly twenty percent. Bound alongside the gapped second variation of \mathcal{E}_q (geodesic vortices), this defines the dual mechanism guaranteeing soliton stability: the aether exponentially dampens inter-loop disturbances at every crossing, while the spectral gap isolates disturbances within the loops themselves.
rem:braid-fluid:
Remark Braid--fluid correspondence: from categorical braiding to vortex dynamics. The categorical braid-group action possesses a direct hydrodynamic interpretation on the brane fluid.

Arnold's geodesic framework. Arnold demonstrated that the Euler equation on (M, g) behaves exactly as the geodesic equation over \mathrm{SDiff}(M) acting under the L^2 metric: \nabla_{\dot\phi}\dot\phi = 0. The velocity vector v = \dot\phi \circ \phi^{-1} solves \partial_t v + \nabla_v v = -\nabla p.

q-deformed diffeomorphisms. The state bundle promotes the classical \mathrm{SDiff}(M) group to \mathrm{SDiff}_q(\mathcal{S}). This imposes two structural shifts:

  1. The L^2 metric upgrades to the Tanaka–Webster inner product. The resulting geodesics solve the quantum Euler equation subject to pressure Q_q.
  2. Confining the state space to flows exhibiting concentrated vorticity across n filaments forces a strict topological quotient onto B_n. The fundamental group of the configuration space \mathrm{Conf}_n(M)/S_n resolves uniquely to B_n.

Braid generators as vortex exchanges. The Artin generator \sigma_i dictates the half-twist spatial exchange of filaments i and i+1. The representation \rho_n(\sigma_i) = \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(i-1)} \otimes c_{V,V} \otimes \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(n-i-1)} (prop:braid-action-tensor) manifests physically as the \mathrm{SU}(2) holonomy traversing the exchange path. rem:planck-reynolds:
Remark Planck--Reynolds number and the turbulence transition. The aether parameter q determines the three Reynolds-number variables in the brane fluid: characteristic velocity c_q = 1/(q-1), characteristic grain scale \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} = (q-1)/q, and dynamic viscosity \nu_q = \hbar_q/2 = (q-1)/(2q).   \mathrm{Re}_q
  = \frac{c_q \cdot \hbar_q}{\nu_q}
  = \frac{2}{q-1}.
Regime q \mathrm{Re}_q Character
Classical \to 1^+ \to \infty Fully turbulent

The aether parameter functions as an inverse turbulence dial. At q = 1, the Reynolds number diverges and unleashes the full Kolmogorov cascade, but the contact structure collapses and particle states vanish.

The laminar--turbulent boundary emerges at \mathrm{Re}_q \sim 1, corresponding to q \sim 3. Active Kelvin modes require [k]_q \leq \mathrm{Re}_q^{1/2}. At the physical anchor q \approx 1.110, this constraint dictates a cutoff k_{\max} \approx 4.
sec:vortex-spectrum-intro:
The q-deformation of brane hydrodynamics forces vortex circulation onto a discrete ladder and pins helicity to a topological invariant. This section collects the modes produced by the braided monoidal structure and the conservation laws it enforces.

It opens with Remark: Vortex intensity modes: from classical fluids to q-deformation, which contrasts four classical mechanisms for discrete vortex spectra with the q-deformed mechanism to anchor the comparison. It then proves Proposition: Discrete vortex mode spectrum — the eigenvalues of the q-Laplacian on a filament are [k]_q^2 \cdot \hbar_q / L_q^2 — and interpret the resulting levels in Remark: Vortex intensity levels as fluid-dynamical orbitals. The central structural result is Proposition: Categorical helicity conservation: helicity operates as a topological invariant of the braided monoidal structure. Remark: Helicity as quantised topological charge reads this invariant as a discrete charge. It closes with Remark: Vortex reconnection as divisor surgery, establishing the birational picture of filament recombination. Remark Vortex intensity modes: from classical fluids to q-deformation. The aether parameter q imposes an algebraic discreteness on vortex circulation absent in classical Navier--Stokes. Four classical mechanisms exhibit discrete modes but continuous intensity; the q-deformation closes this gap.

1. Kelvin waves on vortex filaments. A classical vortex filament supports standing-wave perturbations (Kelvin modes) at discrete wavelengths \lambda_k = L/k, for integers k \geq 1 and filament length L. The dispersion relation reads

  \omega_k =  \frac{\Gamma}{4\pi a^2}k^2
  \bigl(\ln(L/a) - \text{const}\bigr),

with vortex core radius a and circulation \Gamma. These modes are discrete in wave number, yet the circulation \Gamma remains a free continuous parameter. Under q-deformation, the filament inhabits the 1-jet bundle J^1 \mathcal{S}_n, and the q-Laplacian \Delta_q replaces the classical Laplacian.   \omega_k^{(q)} = 
  \frac{\Gamma_q}{4\pi a_q^2}[k]_q^2
  \bigl(\ln_q(L/a_q) - c_q\bigr).

As q \to 1, the q-integers collapse to classical integers, recovering the standard Kelvin spectrum.

In superfluid helium and Bose--Einstein condensates, the macroscopic wave function \psi = |\psi|e^{i\varTheta} forces circulation to quantise as \Gamma_n = n \cdot h/m for n \in \mathbb{Z}. These act as discrete states, not modes. In the brane fluid, the geodesic vortex fixed points of the q-deformed energy functional supply the analogous transitions: each fixed point forms a stable vortex configuration, and transitioning between them requires crossing an energy barrier set by q.

4. Stability eigenvalues. Smooth classical vortex profiles like the Lamb--Oseen vortex possess discrete eigenvalues in their linear stability spectrum. Proposition Categorical helicity conservation. Let (\mathbf{C}, \varTheta, G, \mathcal{S}) be a QOU governed by brane fluid velocity v = \nabla_A S and vorticity \omega = \mathrm{curl}_Av = \nabla_A \times v. Define the categorical helicity of a vortex configuration \{\varrho_1, \ldots, \varrho_n\} as

  \mathcal{H}_q
  = 
  \sum_{i} \oint_{\varrho_i}
  v \cdot \omega\,ds
  + 
  2\sum_{i < j}
  \mathrm{lk}_q(\varrho_i, \varrho_j)
  \Gamma_i^{(q)}\Gamma_j^{(q)},

where \mathrm{lk}_q(\varrho_i, \varrho_j) specifies the q-deformed linking number and \Gamma_i^{(q)} = [j_i]_q[j_i + 1]_q indicates the quantised circulation of filament \varrho_i at intensity level j_i.

Then:

  1. Conservation. The quantum Euler equation strictly conserves \mathcal{H}_q: d\mathcal{H}_q/dt = 0.

  2. Decomposition. The categorical helicity resolves into three distinct topological invariants:

      \mathcal{H}_q
  = 
  \underbrace{\sum_i \mathrm{Wr}_q(\varrho_i)
    (\Gamma_i^{(q)})^2}_{\text{writhe}}
  + 
  \underbrace{\sum_i \mathrm{Tw}_q(\varrho_i)
    (\Gamma_i^{(q)})^2}_{\text{twist}}
  + 
  \underbrace{2\sum_{i<j}
    \mathrm{lk}_q(\varrho_i,\varrho_j)
    \Gamma_i^{(q)}\Gamma_j^{(q)}}_{\text{linking}},

    where \mathrm{Wr}_q and \mathrm{Tw}_q denote the q-deformed writhe and twist obeying the Călugăreanu--White--Fuller relation \mathrm{Wr}_q + \mathrm{Tw}_q = \mathrm{Lk}_q.

  3. Jones polynomial refinement. Classical helicity does not separate knot types. For a single thin tube of flux \Gamma it equals \Gamma^2(\mathrm{Wr} + \mathrm{Tw}) = \Gamma^2\,\mathrm{Lk}, the flux squared times the framing number [moffatt-ricca-helicity]. The value therefore depends on the framing of the tube, not on its knot type: it vanishes exactly for a zero-framed tube, and the unknot and the trefoil both admit zero-framed and non-zero-framed tubes. The Jones polynomial J_L(q) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho(\beta_L)), computed via the Markov trace on the Iwahori--Hecke algebra, acts as a finer invariant. In the brane fluid, it evaluates to:

      J_L(q) =  \exp\!\Bigl(
    \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
    \frac{1}{n}
    \mathrm{tr}\bigl((\check{R})^n\bigr)
    \cdot (q - q^{-1})^n
  \Bigr),

    capturing the full topological structure of the vortex tangle missed by \mathcal{H}_q.

    Where the closure enters, and what is conserved. J_L is a value of the tangle's braid word \beta only after the strands are closed: a cup below and a cap above each strand, the return arcs adding no crossing (closure). Closure is a trace, so it factors through the annular class of \beta in \mathrm{HH}_0 = H_n(q)/[H_n(q), H_n(q)], which keeps every sector character \chi_\lambda; the Markov trace then averages the sectors. Three statements follow directly from the stated input.

    • Isotopy. A smooth ideal flow carries vortex lines with it [moffatt1969], so the closed vortex link at time t is isotopic to the link at time 0. By the Alexander and Markov theorems [alexander1923, markov1936, birman1974] the two braid words are joined by conjugations, stabilisations x \mapsto x\,\sigma_n^{\pm 1} and their inverses. Along such a path the Markov trace changes only by the recorded stabilisation factors, so the normalised value J_L is conserved.
    • Fixed axis. If the tangle stays a closed braid on the same strands around a fixed axis, the path uses conjugations only. Then the whole annular class is conserved, and with it every sector character, which is finer than J_L. Under stabilisation the strand number changes and only the Markov-normalised value survives.
    • Reconnection. A reconnection replaces one crossing \sigma by \sigma^{-1} and breaks isotopy. By the skein relation \sigma - \sigma^{-1} = q - q^{-1}, every closure invariant jumps by exactly q - q^{-1} times its value on the word with that crossing smoothed.

    The two inputs to the isotopy statement, frozen-in vortex lines and Markov's theorem, are cited and not proved here. The classical counterpart of closing the strands is the asymptotic linking number, where long orbit segments are closed by short paths whose contribution vanishes in the limit [komendarczyk2008].

  4. Classical limit. As q \to 1, the representations collapse ([j]_q[j+1]_q \to j(j+1)), linking reduces to Gauss linking (\mathrm{lk}_q \to \mathrm{lk}), and \mathcal{H}_q simplifies to classical Moffatt helicity H = \int v \cdot \omega\,dV.

rem:helicity-physical:
Remark Helicity as quantised topological charge. The conservation of categorical helicity physically manifests topological charge conservation within the fluid. Under smooth inviscid (Euler) evolution, vortex lines are transported by the flow, so the evolution cannot alter the total helicity of a vortex configuration: helicity is preserved by every volume-preserving diffeomorphism, and it equals the average asymptotic linking number of pairs of trajectories [khesin2003, Thm. 2.2, Thm. 2.5]. It merely redistributes helicity among writhe, twist, and linking, as demonstrated by trefoil chirality flips. The statement does not extend to viscous flow. For Navier--Stokes with viscosity \nu > 0 the helicity H = \int v \cdot \omega\,dV obeys dH/dt = -2\nu \int \omega \cdot \mathrm{curl}\,\omega\,dV, which has no sign and does not vanish in general, and vortex lines of any knot or link type can reconnect while the solution stays smooth [enciso2017].

The exact quantisation of \Gamma_i^{(q)} = [j_i]_q[j_i+1]_q mandates that each term in the helicity sum remains individually quantised. Consequently, helicity is restricted to a discrete lattice structured by the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) representation labels \{j_i\}.

Two sources bound helicity by energy, and in both the bound is geometric, not topological. For a smooth field V on a compact domain \Omega of \mathbb{R}^3, S^3 or H^3, the Biot--Savart operator gives |H(V)| \le N(R)\,\|V\|^2, where N(R) depends only on the radius R of a ball with the volume of \Omega [deturck-gluck2008, §13, Thm. 7]. That note states it gives only a hint of the proofs in S^3 and H^3, so its constants are to be checked against the journal version before any use. When the pairwise linking numbers vanish, as for a Borromean configuration, the pairwise helicities H_{12} = \mathrm{lk}(L_1,L_2)\,\mathrm{Flux}(B_1)\,\mathrm{Flux}(B_2) are zero [komendarczyk2008, §6, eq. (6.1)], and the invariant that remains is the third-order helicity. On Borromean flux tubes it equals \bar\mu_{123}(L)\,\mathrm{Flux}(B_1)\,\mathrm{Flux}(B_2)\,\mathrm{Flux}(B_3) [komendarczyk2008, §6, eq. (6.6)], so it is cubic in the fluxes, not quadratic, and it is totally antisymmetric in the three components because \bar\mu_{123} is [komendarczyk2008, Rem. 2.3]. Its bound by the L^2-energy, |H_{123}(B;T)| \le C_T\,E_2(B)^{3/2}, has a constant set by the geometry of the invariant domain, and the source records that the estimate is meaningless once the handlebodies come close to one another [komendarczyk2008, §7, Thm. 7.1 and eqs. (7.6)--(7.7)]. The Freedman--He lower bound quoted there, eq.~(7.8), sums over components, each component taken against the whole link, and carries the pure constant (\pi/16)^{1/4} with no volume factor. These are statements about smooth fields; they bound the classical helicity and say nothing about the quantised labels \Gamma_i^{(q)}.

Remark Vortex reconnection as divisor surgery. When two vortex filaments approach, the divisor \{\psi = 0\} undergoes surgery. In smooth inviscid (Euler) flow, vortex lines are transported by the flow and their link type is fixed, so a change of topology is incompatible with smoothness there. Viscous reconnection carries no such obstruction: there exist smooth solutions of the three-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations in which vortex lines and vortex tubes of arbitrary knot and link type are created and destroyed in arbitrarily short time [enciso2017]. Reconnection by itself is therefore compatible with smooth classical viscous flow, and the role assigned here to the quantum pressure Q_q is to organise the surgery. Let D = \sum_i n_i\varrho_i denote the effective divisor framing the vortex configuration, where \varrho_i represent the filament components and n_i \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z} identify their intensity levels. Reconnection constitutes a birational transformation on the divisor:

  D =  \cdots + \varrho_i + \varrho_j + \cdots
  \quad\xrightarrow{\text{surgery}}\quad
  D' =  \cdots + \varrho_i' + \varrho_j' + \cdots,

where \varrho_i' and \varrho_j' designate the reconnected filaments. The surgery preserves three quantities:

  • Total circulation: \Gamma_i^{(q)} + \Gamma_j^{(q)} = \Gamma_{i'}^{(q)} + \Gamma_{j'}^{(q)} (enforcing conservation of the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) Casimir).
  • Categorical helicity: \mathcal{H}_q[D] = \mathcal{H}_q[D'] (helicity conservation), although writhe and twist are free to redistribute. The redistribution is forced whenever the exchange acts as a crossing change between distinct filaments a \neq b of a pure braid. A crossing change of sign \epsilon = \pm 1 moves \mathrm{lk}(\varrho_a, \varrho_b) by exactly -\epsilon and the mutual helicity \sum_{a \neq b} \mathrm{lk}\,\Gamma_a\Gamma_b by exactly -2\epsilon\,\Gamma_a\Gamma_b, while the Reidemeister II and III moves leave both unchanged. Conservation of the total therefore requires an equal and opposite change in the writhe-plus-twist term, which is the transfer from linking to coiling observed in reconnecting vortex links [scheeler2014].
  • Total homology class: [D] = [D'] evaluated in H_1(\mathcal{S}).

The first two classes map exactly to the two eigenvalues of the Hecke relation (T - q)(T + q^{-1}) = 0, explicitly verifying the braid--fluid correspondence.   = 
  C_q\varepsilon^{2/3}
  \frac{[k]_q^{-5/3}}{[k]_q / k},

    where \varepsilon represents the energy dissipation rate, C_q acts as a q-dependent Kolmogorov constant, and the ratio [k]_q / k corrects for the non-uniform spacing of q-integers.       T_{k \to k+1}
  = 
  \varepsilon
  \frac{[k+1]_q^{2/3} - [k]_q^{2/3}}
       {[k+1]_q - [k]_q}.

    For large k, the denominator scales as [k+1]_q - [k]_q \sim q^k \cdot q/(q+1). The transfer rate thus drops exponentially at high wavenumbers, enforcing a strict structural UV cutoff.

      N_{\mathrm{modes}}
   \leq

  =

    \frac{3}{4}
    \frac{\ln(2/(q-1))}{\ln q}
  \biggr\rfloor.

    The bound is the logarithmic form of the dissipation-scale cutoff q^{N_{\mathrm{modes}}} \leq \mathrm{Re}_q^{3/4} (every active mode lies below the Kolmogorov scale), which is the modeling hypothesis of the derivation; the passage from the cutoff to the stated bound is elementary. At the physical anchor q \approx 1.110, N_{\mathrm{modes}} \approx 21. (This accounts for all modes spanning the cascade; the Planck--Reynolds bound k_{\max} \approx 4 measures only those modes carrying significant amplitude.)

Remark Derivation of the Kelvin dispersion from the q-Laplacian eigenvalue problem. Setup. Let \varrho describe a stable vortex filament of length L in the brane fluid, parametrised by arc length s \in [0, L] under periodic boundary conditions \varrho(0) = \varrho(L). Let \eta(s, t) denote a small normal displacement of the filament from equilibrium (a Kelvin wave). The linearised q-Navier--Stokes equation governing normal perturbations of \varrho reads

  \partial_t^2 \eta
  = 
  \frac{\Gamma_q}{4\pi a_q^2}\Delta_q\eta
  -  \nu_q\Delta_q\partial_t \eta,

where \Gamma_q = [j]_q[j+1]_q fixes the quantised circulation at intensity level j, a_q specifies the q-deformed vortex core radius, and the trailing term applies viscous damping.

The q-Laplacian eigenvalue problem. The q-Laplacian evaluated on a circle of length L acts exclusively on L-periodic functions f(s). Its eigenvalue problem reads

  \Delta_qf_k
  =  -\mu_kf_k,
  \qquad
  f_k(s + L) = f_k(s).

For the classical Laplacian (q = 1) in arc length s, the eigenfunctions are e^{2\pi i k s / L} with eigenvalues \mu_k = (2\pi k/L)^2. The q-Laplacian replaces the integer k with the q-integer [k]_q = (q^k - q^{-k})/(q - q^{-1}). The derivation below works in the variable z = e^{2\pi i s / L}, where the eigenvalue is the dimensionless

  \mu_k^{(q)}
  = 
  [k]_q^2 .

The arc-length factor (2\pi/L)^2 is a change of unit, not part of the algebraic operator. All units are restored at once by the single factor \hbar_q / L_q^2 below. So L_q is the length in that normalisation: matching \hbar_q times the arc-length eigenvalue (2\pi[k]_q/L)^2 sets L_q = L/(2\pi), whereas writing (2\pi[k]_q/L_q)^2 at L_q = L would differ from \lambda_k^{(q)} below by the factor 4\pi^2/\hbar_q.

Derivation. The q-derivative operators define the q-Laplacian. Assign z = e^{2\pi i s / L} for a function f on the circle. Then:

  D_q f(z) = \frac{f(qz) - f(q^{-1}z)}{(q - q^{-1})z},

and \Delta_q = -zD_q \circ zD_q (composing the radial part of the q-Casimir). Operating on the monomial z^k yields

  D_q(z^k)
  = \frac{q^k z^k - q^{-k} z^k}{(q - q^{-1})z}
  = [k]_qz^{k-1}.

Consequently zD_q(z^k) = [k]_qz^k, proving

  \Delta_q(z^k) = -[k]_q^2z^k.

  = 
  [k]_q^2 \cdot \frac{\hbar_q}{L_q^2}.

  -\omega^2
  =

  +  i\omega\nu_q\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}.

In the undamped limit (\nu_q = 0, tracing the Euler limit), the dispersion relation simplifies to

  \omega_k^{(q)}
  = 
  \frac{\Gamma_q^{1/2}}{2\sqrt{\pi}a_q}
  \frac{[k]_q}{L_q},

producing the q-deformed Kelvin dispersion. In the damped regime (\nu_q > 0), the complex frequency isolates the decay rate

  \gamma_k^{(q)}
  = 
  \frac{\nu_q}{2}\frac{[k]_q^2}{L_q^2}
  =
